Statistical equilibrium of atomic level populations (∑j=i​(nj​Rji​−ni​Rij​)=0)

Words: 56
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
An atomic population is in statistical equilibrium when the total rate into each level equals the total rate out, subject to conservation of the total number of atoms or ions. The rates can include electron-impact transitions and spontaneous emission. This is weaker than thermodynamic equilibrium: a collisionally excited, radiatively decaying dilute gas generally does not have Boltzmann level populations.

Auger effect

Words: 58 Articles: 1
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
A transition filling an inner atomic vacancy can transfer its released energy to another bound electron, ejecting it instead of emitting a photon. This provides an atomic relaxation channel following electron capture and ionization.

Auger electron

Words: 27
Auger effect OurBigBook.com
An electron ejected by the Auger effect. Its kinetic energy is determined mainly by the atomic levels involved, rather than directly by the energy of the radiation that created the original vacancy.

Spectral line profile (φ(ν))

Words: 182 Articles: 3
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
A normalized spectral line profile distributes a transition's emission or absorption over frequency, with ∫φ(ν)dν=1 and units Hz−1. Thermal motion, finite excited-state lifetime and collisions can give different contributions to the shape. Normalization lets an optically thin integrated line measure the relevant column density without requiring the detailed profile.

Spectral line strength (S=∫κν​dν)

Words: 55
Spectral line profile OurBigBook.com
The integrated absorption coefficient of an isolated spectral line is its line strength. For a mass coefficient write κν​=Sϕν​, where ∫ϕν​dν=1. The units of S include the chosen spectral-coordinate unit; a strength integrated over wavenumber is not numerically interchangeable with one integrated over frequency. Changing normalized width at fixed strength redistributes opacity without changing its spectral integral.

Lorentz line shape (κν​=πS​(ν−ν0​)2+Δ2Δ​)

Words: 85 Articles: 1
Spectral line profile OurBigBook.com
A normalized collisional line model κν​=(S/π)Δ/[(ν−ν0​)2+Δ2], with integrated strength S and half-width Δ. The centre scales as S/Δ and far wings as SΔ/(ν−ν0​)2. In a dilute pressure-broadened gas Δ scales approximately with pressure.

Strong-line limit (C≫1)

Words: 49
Lorentz line shape OurBigBook.com
A regime where optical-depth-one transmission occurs in the far wings of a strongly absorbing line. With a uniformly mixed absorber, Δ=Δs​p/ps​ and C=qSps​/(2πgΔs​)≫1, the radiative-wing optical depth is τ≃qSΔs​p2/[2πgps​(ν−ν0​)2]. This condition does not make pressure broadening valid in the arbitrarily rarefied upper atmosphere.

Gross atomic structure (En​∼−α2μc2/(2n2))

Words: 39
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
Gross atomic structure denotes the leading nonrelativistic Coulomb binding levels, before fine and hyperfine splittings. For a hydrogenic two-body system, the reduced mass controls the binding energy and characteristic separation. Fine structure is smaller by roughly α2; nuclear magnetic hyperfine effects have an additional electron-to-nuclear mass suppression.

Positronium

Words: 97 Articles: 1
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
Positronium is the electromagnetic bound state of an electron and a Positron. Their equal masses give reduced mass me​/2, half the hydrogenic Rydberg binding scale and approximately twice the electron-proton separation of hydrogen. Its spin singlet and triplet differ in hyperfine energy; annihilation also affects their physical lifetimes and splitting.

Positronium Zeeman spectrum (E±​=−A/4±21​A2+16μB2​B2​)

Words: 52
Positronium OurBigBook.com
For the dimensionless-spin Hamiltonian ASe​⋅Sp​+2μB​B(Sez​−Spz​), the two aligned-spin states remain at A/4. The two states of total spin projection zero mix and have the displayed energies. The parameter 4μB​B/A compares off-diagonal Zeeman mixing in the singlet-triplet basis with half the zero-field splitting. A crossover is gradual, not a level-crossing phase transition.

Central field approximation

Words: 43 Articles: 1
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
A many-electron atomic environment is replaced by a spherically averaged one-electron potential. Radial screening changes the Coulomb attraction and produces orbitals labelled by radial and angular quantum numbers. This spherical approximation and the separate self-consistency step in the Hartree method are related but distinct assumptions.

Spherical averaging versus self-consistent orbital optimization

Central field approximation OurBigBook.com

Magnetic dipole transition

Words: 53
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
A transition driven by an oscillating magnetic field through H′=−μ⋅B. The rank-one magnetic operator preserves parity and allows changes in total angular momentum of zero or one, excluding zero-to-zero. Its spherical components select changes in the angular momentum component of 0,±1. Hyperfine clock states can therefore couple even when each has zero first-order static magnetic moment.

Optical dipole trap

Words: 61
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
A far-detuned laser produces an atomic AC Stark shift approximately U=−Reα(ω)∣E0​∣2/4. Its spatial gradient creates a conservative dipole force. For a suitable red-detuned ground-state atom, high intensity is an energy minimum and can confine several hyperfine states without relying on nonzero permanent magnetic moments. Photon scattering, differential light shifts and intensity noise remain limitations. This atomic use is more specific than a general dielectric-particle optical trap.

Charge exchange

Words: 17
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
Transfer of one or more electrons between a moving particle and its surroundings, changing the particle charge state.

Electronic excitation

Words: 18
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
Transfer of a system to an excited electronic state. Energy deposited into electrons need not become a permanent atomic displacement.

Atomic term (2S+1L)

Words: 90 Articles: 2
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
An LS coupling multiplet with specified total orbital angular momentum L and total spin S, usually within a specified electron configuration. Its magnetic states have ML​=−L,…,L and MS​=−S,…,S. Spin-orbit coupling splits it into atomic fine-structure levels.

Doublet term (S=1/2,2L)

Words: 38
Atomic term OurBigBook.com
An atomic term with total spin one half and spin multiplicity two. A doublet S term has only J=1/2, while a doublet with nonzero L can have J=L-1/2 and J=L+1/2. Spin multiplicity therefore need not equal the number of resolved spectral lines.

Atomic fine-structure level (2S+1LJ​)

Words: 24
Atomic term OurBigBook.com
A level of an atomic term with specified total angular momentum J. Without an external field, its 2J+1 magnetic states remain degenerate in a rotationally invariant Hamiltonian.

Hydrogen-like ion

Words: 20
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
A monatomic ion with exactly one electron. Its nonrelativistic Coulomb potential energy levels scale as Z2 at fixed principal quantum number, apart from reduced mass corrections.

Term symbol (2S+1LJ​)

Words: 73
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
In LS coupling, an atomic term symbol specifies total electronic spin S, total orbital angular momentum L, and total angular momentum J. The superscript 2S+1 is the spin multiplicity; the letters S,P,D,F,… denote L=0,1,2,3,…. Coupling gives J=∣L−S∣,…,L+S, and a fixed-J level has 2J+1 magnetic substates before an external field resolves them. For example, 3P has S=L=1 and levels J=0,1,2, containing 1+3+5=9 states altogether. A term symbol does not itself specify the radial electron configuration.

Rydberg atom (n≫1)

Words: 63 Articles: 1
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
A Rydberg atom has an electron excited to a high principal quantum number.

Rydberg blockade

Words: 53
Rydberg atom OurBigBook.com
Rydberg blockade suppresses simultaneous excitation of nearby chemical atoms into strongly interacting Rydberg atom states. If the interaction shifts the doubly excited level by much more than the excitation linewidth and coherent drive scale, a pulse resonant for one isolated chemical atom becomes off-resonant when a neighbour is already excited. The resulting conditional dynamics can implement an entangling two-qubit gate for neutral-atom qubits.

Selection rule

Words: 41 Articles: 1
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
A restriction on transitions between quantum states for a specified interaction. An electric-dipole selection rule is one example.

Spin selection rule (ΔS=0)

Selection rule OurBigBook.com
In the nonrelativistic electric-dipole approximation, the dipole operator does not act on spin, so transitions between different total-spin states vanish. Spin–orbit coupling can give such transitions weak intensity.

Lamb shift

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
A quantum electrodynamics correction separates hydrogen atom levels such as 2s1/2​ and 2p1/2​ that coincide in the simplest model.
The Lamb shift measures an energy level displacement beyond a specified Dirac equation reference. In the point-proton, infinite-nuclear-mass Coulomb potential model, 2S1/2​ and 2P1/2​ share principal quantum number n=2 and total electronic angular momentum j=1/2, hence energy, despite differing orbital angular momentum values.[ref]
The Lamb-Retherford experiment converts a small energy difference into a large detector change: prepare a long-lived quantum state, transfer population into a short-lived one, and read the surviving beam.

Hydrogen Lamb splitting (νL​=[E(2S1/2​)−E(2P1/2​)]/h)

Words: 68
Lamb shift OurBigBook.com
The zero-field energy levels here are averaged over hyperfine structure; h is the Planck constant. Electron self-energy and vacuum polarization produce radiative corrections. Self-energy describes the bound electron's radiative interaction with its own electromagnetic field. Precision predictions also include nuclear recoil and proton charge radius effects; assigning recoil terms to the reference or Lamb shift is convention-dependent. A finite proton charge radius changes binding independently of radiative effects.[ref]
A vacuum-electric field “jiggling” picture motivates one contribution, not every hydrogen atom energy correction.

Lamb-Retherford experiment

Words: 855 Articles: 2
Lamb shift OurBigBook.com
In 1947, Willis Eugene Lamb Jr. and Robert Curtis Retherford dissociated hydrogen in a tungsten oven, crossed its atomic jet with electrons for collisional excitation, and detected surviving 2S atoms by electron ejection from metal. An electrometer and galvanometer read the current. They interrupted fixed-frequency microwaves while sweeping the static magnetic field; a flip coil calibrated the field. Their Zeeman splitting comparison placed 2S1/2​ about 1000 MHz above 2P1/2​; the plotted 1000 MHz displacement was explicitly not a best fit.[ref]
The 1955 lecture's apparatus cross-section identifies movable slits, an electron bombarder, a radiofrequency transmission line with beam slots, a d.c. quenching electrode, metal target, electron collector, and magnet poles. A 2S→2P transition followed by rapid spontaneous emission leaves a ground-state atom unable to eject detector electrons. The scan holds radiofrequency and amplitude fixed. Natural linewidth and unresolved hyperfine structure broaden resonances, whose analysis yields zero-field separations.[ref]
Static electric field quenching supplied a control. The 1947 report identifies natural linewidth, hyperfine structure, excessive microwave intensity, and field inhomogeneity as width contributions, and flags imperfect magnetic calibration. It does not specify an absolute microwave-frequency calibration procedure.[ref]
The surname is Robert Curtis Retherford's: “Retherford” and “Rutherford” name different people. The historical Lamb-Retherford experiment should retain the former spelling.[ref]

Lamb shift quenching readout (Q=(Ioff​−Ion​)/(Ioff​−Ibg​))

Words: 175
Lamb-Retherford experiment OurBigBook.com
For a simple original detector model, let ΦS​ be the incident rate of surviving 2S atoms, e the positive elementary charge, η the mean number of collected electrons per incident 2S atom, and Ibg​ a stable background current. Take current magnitudes as positive. If microwaves remove a fraction p before the target,
Ioff​=Ibg​+eηΦS​,Ion​=Ibg​+eηΦS​(1−p),Q=p.
(1)
The equality needs the same beam flux, background and collection efficiency in both measurements. It is an ideal interpretation of a normalized current loss, not a claim that an actual galvanometer directly counts individual transitions. Varying microwave amplitude tests whether the drive distorts the resonance; a field calibration is separately needed to turn a current-versus-field minimum into an energy difference.
The metastable atomic level matters because an electric-dipole selection rule suppresses the direct 2S→1S electric-dipole interaction, whereas the opposite-parity 2S↔2P transition can be driven. A long lifetime can store the prepared population until interrogation. After transfer to 2P, a short lifetime supplies the loss mechanism and a broad natural linewidth. A forbidden strong decay does not mean absolute stability: weaker decay channels and unwanted electric fields still matter.

This local linear model omits hyperfine structure and nonlinear level mixing; it is not the historical hydrogen Zeeman splitting calculation.
Use a Lorentzian line shape for a weak-drive current dip,
I(B)=C−1+4(B−Br​)2/wB2​A​,wB​=∣a∣wν​​.

If an exponential decay with lifetime τ alone set this width, natural linewidth would give wν​=1/(2πτ) and τ≃1.59 ns. The chosen width is an explanatory input, not a measurement of a historical lifetime.
Generate 65 equally spaced fields from 2 to 18 mT and add independent Gaussian noise with known standard deviation σI​=0.004 signal units. A simultaneous nonlinear regression fit of C,A,Br​,wB​ gives Br​≃10.0007 mT, wB​≃4.9305 mT and ν0​≃1099.986 MHz. With residual derivatives Jik​=∂I(Bi​)/∂θk​ and θ=(C,A,Br​,wB​), the local covariance matrix estimate is

This uses the stipulated noise variance and a local linear approximation, rather than treating the width as the centre error. Repeated noisy samples can locate a broad line's centre much more closely than its width.

u2(ν0​)≃a2u2(Br​)+a2ub2​+(aBr​)2ug2​+ud2​.

Here u denotes a standard uncertainty, not a frequency. The four contributions in MHz are 0.285, 0.400, 0.200, and 0.100; adding their squares gives u(ν0​)≃0.540 MHz. The calibration offset shifts all sampled fields together, so increasing the sample count cannot average it away. Uncertainty in a, unresolved components, asymmetric line distortion, and errors in the assumed field dependence would require additional terms or a richer model. Zeeman splitting

Words: 2k Articles: 18
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
Zeeman splitting is the separation of energy levels or mode frequencies by a background magnetic field. In atomic physics, the magnetic field couples to a magnetic dipole moment, lifting quantum degeneracy. Transitions between the shifted quantum states can turn one spectral line into several. A split level and a split spectral line are different objects: the emitted photon measures the difference between two level energies, and the electric-dipole selection rule determines which differences appear.
The Stern-Gerlach experiment also probes magnetic dipole moments, through beam deflection in a magnetic field gradient. Here the readout is a spectral line.
The pattern makes an invisible magnetic field visible through spectroscopy. It also reveals angular momentum and magnetic dipole moments inside chemical atoms. Zeeman slowers exploit a changing resonance frequency to keep moving chemical atoms absorbing laser photons; a magneto-optical trap combines position-dependent shifts with electromagnetic polarization and laser cooling. Related mode shifts occur in Zeeman splitting of an antiferromagnetic spin wave.

Zeeman shift (ΔE=gF​mF​μB​B)

Words: 67
Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
The change of an energy level in a magnetic field. The displayed weak-field form applies to a hyperfine level with magnetic projection mF​, when gF​ is the corresponding Landé g-factor. A transition shift is the difference of the two level shifts divided by Planck constant. A clock transition can have zero first-order transition shift even when its two individual level slopes are nonzero. For mF​=0 hyperfine levels, the linear level shift vanishes and quadratic terms remain.

Transverse orbital Zeeman mixing (E±​=(Et​+E0​)/2±(Et​−E0​)2/4+(μB​B)2​)

Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
For an axially split p multiplet with pz​ energy E0​ and equal px​,py​ energies Et​, a transverse x-directed magnetic field leaves px​ unchanged and couples py​,pz​ through the orbital angular momentum operator Lx​. The matrix element has modulus μB​B, giving the two energy eigenvalues in the title. For μB​B≪∣Et​−E0​∣, the orbital shifts are quadratic despite a linear Zeeman energy operator. A full quadratic-field calculation also includes the diamagnetic term; electron spin gives its own linear contribution.

Zeeman populations from an unpolarized angular-momentum multiplet (p(mL​,mS​)=⟨mL​,mS​∣PJ​∣mL​,mS​⟩/(2J+1))

Words: 130
Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
An equal incoherent mixture within a fixed total-J multiplet has density operator ρ=PJ​/(2J+1), where PJ​ is its orthogonal projection. If the applied-field Hamiltonian operator is proportional to Lz​+2Sz​ and no spin-orbit interaction is retained, its energy eigenstates are the uncoupled states ∣mL​,mS​⟩. The Born rule gives their populations by the formula above, or equivalently by squared Clebsch-Gordan decomposition coefficients. Equal populations of coupled states need not give equal populations of magnetic energy eigenvalues.
For L=1,S=1/2,J=3/2, the nonextremal coupled states have weights 2/3 and 1/3 in their two uncoupled components. The five dimensionless magnetic energies −2,−1,0,1,2 then have populations 1/4,1/6,1/6,1/6,1/4; the zero energy contains two independent states, each with population 1/12. In a different, weak-field approximation with a dominant spin-orbit interaction, projecting into the isolated multiplet gives the Landé g-factor spectrum instead. The full operator and its projection must not be interchanged.

Zeeman discovery experiment of 1896

Words: 383
Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
In August 1896, Pieter Zeeman observed broadened sodium spectral lines at Leiden, initially without resolved components. His lecture describes a slit and concave diffraction grating, then compares the broadening with the sodium doublet separation: about one thirtieth, roughly 0.2 ångström. This supplied a spectral reference scale, not an absolute magnetic field calibration. Later cadmium photographs displayed resolved transverse triplets and axial doublets.[ref]
The fuller report specifies a concave diffraction grating of ten-foot radius with 14,438 lines per inch, an adjustable slit and a micrometer eyepiece with vertical crosswire. Salt in a flame between electromagnet poles supplied the sodium spectral lines. Repeated switching broadened and restored them. To test changes in flame temperature or vapour density, Pieter Zeeman examined photon absorption through a heated porcelain tube with water-cooled glass windows. The arc lamp was displaced from the magnet and its light redirected by a mirror to avoid disturbing the arc. Rotating a narrower tube made the absorption spectral lines equally broad at different heights; the magnetic field still broadened their whole length.[ref]
For the axial test, pierced electromagnet poles let the light travel along the magnetic field. A quarter-wave plate and polarizer selected one broadened edge; rotating the analyser by 90∘ or reversing the magnet current exchanged the visible edge. The crosswire made its displacement detectable. This tested electromagnetic polarization as well as line width. For its rough estimate the report compared each side's widening with the sodium doublet separation, obtaining about one fortieth, and stated an approximate magnetic field intensity in historical units. These passages give no absolute field-calibration procedure; the inferred charge-to-mass ratio was explicitly a first approximation.[ref]
Hendrik Antoon Lorentz's charged-oscillator theory connected the observed splitting to moving electric charge. In modern language, a line-position measurement needs a wavelength or frequency calibration and an independent magnetic field calibration before it determines a magnetic dipole moment. Resolving the individual components adds the transition information used in the worked example below.

Weak-field Zeeman splitting (ΔE=μB​gJ​mJ​B)

Words: 317 Articles: 1
Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
Use the leading nonrelativistic magnetic coupling for an electronic level with total angular momentum operator J, and choose the z axis along a uniform external magnetic field B=Bz^, B≥0. Write its magnetic quantum number as mJ​, so Jz​∣J,mJ​⟩=ℏmJ​∣J,mJ​⟩. There are 2J+1 possibilities from −J to J. With Landé g-factor gJ​, the first-order shift is
ΔE=μB​gJ​mJ​B,μB​=2me​eℏ​,Δνul​=hμB​B​(gu​mu​−gl​ml​).
(5)
Here e>0 is the magnitude of the electron electric charge, me​ its mass, h the Planck constant, and μB​ the Bohr magneton. Both gJ​ and mJ​ are dimensionless; with B measured in tesla and μB​ in joules per tesla, ΔE is in joules. The photon frequency shift Δνul​ is in hertz, not angular frequency; indices u,l denote upper and lower levels. NIST states this weak-field convention and its orbital/spin assumptions explicitly.[ref]
The sign follows directly from magnetic dipole potential energy. Within this electronic J multiplet, the projected magnetic dipole moment is μ=−gJ​μB​J/ℏ. Therefore HZ​=−μ⋅B has the displayed positive coefficient. Subtracting the shifts of the two levels and using photon energy hνul​=Eu​−El​ gives the transition formula. For the orbital case, μB​/h=e/(4πme​) gives the same leading frequency spacing as the classical charged oscillator. This explains the historical sensitivity to charge divided by mass; the quantum state derivation here is modern.
“Weak” compares interaction energies: mixing with neighbouring fine structure levels must be small, so J remains a useful quantum number. The formula keeps the term linear in B and neglects quadratic shifts. It also omits hyperfine structure; if that is resolved and controls the coupling, the appropriate total electronic-plus-nuclear angular momentum and splitting factor must replace J,gJ​. Weak compared with fine structure does not automatically mean weak compared with hyperfine structure.

Weak-field Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
The Zeeman effect need not be diagonal between different J multiplets. The familiar Landé g-factor gives the interaction projected into one isolated multiplet. Inter-multiplet matrix elements cause higher-order weak-field shifts and become important in the Paschen-Back effect.

Normal Zeeman effect (Δν=0,±μB​B/h)

Words: 266
Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
The normal Zeeman effect is the simple three-frequency pattern obtained in the orbital limit. Assume negligible net spin, negligible hyperfine structure and quadratic shifts, and an allowed electric-dipole interaction between levels with orbital splitting factor one. A level with J=0 has only mJ​=0 and no first-order shift. For the other levels, gJ​=1 gives ΔE=μB​mJ​B. Define q=mu​−ml​, rather than the final-minus-initial change of the emitting atom. The electric-dipole selection rule allows q=0,±1, hence
νul​=ν0​+qδνB​,δνB​=hμB​B​.
(6)
Many allowed transitions can share one frequency; a triplet need not mean exactly three transitions. The cleanest illustrative example is Ju​=1→Jl​=0, with three upper quantum states and one unshifted lower quantum state. The q=0 component is called π, and q=±1 components σ± with this stated convention. During emission the atom changes its magnetic quantum number by −q.
For an original numerical example choose B=0.50 T and a zero-field vacuum wavelength λ0​=500 nm. Using μB​≃9.27401×10−24 JT−1 and h=6.62607015×10−34 Js gives δνB​≃7.00 GHz. The two outer components are separated by 2δνB​≃14.0 GHz. Differentiating the vacuum relation λ=c/ν, with c the speed of light, gives
Δλq​≃−cλ02​​qδνB​.
(7)
Each outer component lies about 0.00584 nm from the centre. Positive q means higher frequency and shorter wavelength. Equal spacing in frequency is only approximately equal spacing in wavelength. These are calculated values for a chosen model, not historical measurements.

Polarization of Zeeman components

Words: 279
Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
Viewed perpendicular to the magnetic field, the normal Zeeman effect has a π component with linear polarization parallel to the magnetic field and two σ components polarized perpendicular to it. Along the magnetic field, π vanishes and the σ pair has opposite circular polarizations. Pieter Zeeman described these geometry-dependent patterns in his lecture.[ref]
The geometry can be derived from electric dipole radiation. Let the observation unit vector be n=(sinθ,0,cosθ), with θ measured from the magnetic field. Radiation retains only the transverse part of the oscillating electric dipole moment d:
Erad​ ∝ d−n(n⋅d).
(8)
For π, take d∥z^; its angular light intensity factor is sin2θ, so it vanishes on axis. For σ±, use normalized complex dipoles (x^±iy^​)/2​. Their angular factors are (1+cos2θ)/2. Projection gives circles on axis, lines at θ=π/2, and generally elliptical polarization between. These factors assume equal dipole magnitudes; actual line light intensities also depend on initial quantum state populations, transition strengths and collection geometry. No absolute handedness name is needed: it depends on the viewing and phase conventions.
A transverse polarizer can separate π from σ even before the spectral line components are fully resolved. Along the magnetic field, a quarter-wave plate followed by a polarizer converts the two opposite circular polarizations into distinguishable linear settings. This explains why polarization analysis carried information beyond a small increase in line width.

Landé g-factor (gJ​)

Words: 157 Articles: 1
Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
The Landé g-factor is the dimensionless electronic magnetic splitting factor relating a level's magnetic dipole moment to its total angular momentum. In the approximation where total orbital angular momentum L and total spin S couple to J=L+S, take the orbital factor as one and the electron spin factor as gs​≃2. For J>0,
gJ​=1+(gs​−1)2J(J+1)J(J+1)+S(S+1)−L(L+1)​.
(9)
This follows by projecting L+gs​S=J+(gs​−1)S onto J and using 2S⋅J=J2+S2−L2. At S=0, it gives gJ​=1; at L=0 and J=S, it gives gJ​=gs​. A J=0 level instead has zero first-order electronic shift; the formula's zero denominator must not be used. This gJ​ is distinct from the statistical weight of an atomic level 2J+1, sometimes also written gJ​.

Zeeman spacing of a single f electron (ΔE=(6/7)μB​B)

Words: 39
Landé g-factor OurBigBook.com
For a free ion with one f electron in its weak-field ground multiplet, L=3,S=1/2,J=5/2 and gJ​=6/7. The six magnetic substates have adjacent spacing gJ​μB​B and full spread 5gJ​μB​B. A crystal field can change the applicable effective low-energy description.

Anomalous Zeeman effect

Words: 417 Articles: 3
Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
The anomalous Zeeman effect is Zeeman splitting whose pattern is not the simple orbital triplet. Spin and spin-orbit interaction make the upper and lower Landé g-factors differ. The same weak-field formula still applies when its assumptions hold: “anomalous” does not mean nonlinear in the magnetic field.
For example, take an electronic transition with Lu​=1,Su​=1/2,Ju​=1/2 and Ll​=0,Sl​=1/2,Jl​=1/2, neglecting hyperfine structure. With gs​=2, the formula above gives gu​=2/3 and gl​=2. The two allowed q=0 transitions have dimensionless shifts gu​mu​−gl​ml​=±2/3, while the q=±1 transitions give ±4/3. Thus there are four frequencies, even though each level contains only two magnetic quantum numbers. This is an independent worked deduction; it should not be substituted for the unresolved widths in the 1896 experiment.

Words: 197 Articles: 1
Anomalous Zeeman effect OurBigBook.com
Neglect hyperfine structure and use a magnetic field weak compared with the spin-orbit interaction. The sodium D doublet has transitions 3p2P1/2​→3s2S1/2​ and 3p2P3/2​→3s2S1/2​. Their Landé g-factors are 2/3, 4/3 and 2 respectively. With mu​,ml​ denoting upper and lower magnetic labels, the photon shift is
δEγ​=μB​B(gu​mu​−2ml​),mu​−ml​=0,±1.
(10)
The first transition has four allowed shifts μB​B{±2/3,±4/3}; the second has six, μB​B{±1/3,±1,±5/3}. The most blue-shifted component of the second is mu​=1/2→ml​=−1/2, with shift 5μB​B/3. The apparently larger shift mu​=3/2→ml​=−1/2 is excluded by the electric-dipole selection rule. The 3p2P3/2​ level lies above 3p2P1/2​, so in this weak-field model the 5/3 component also has the shortest wavelength of the whole doublet. [ref]

A drawing without a labelled energy axis can still estimate B if it includes both unsplit D lines with known wavelengths: their separation calibrates hc(1/λ2​−1/λ1​). Anomalous Zeeman effect OurBigBook.com
For the electronic 2S1/2​→2P1/2​ transition, neglect hyperfine structure and use weak-field LS coupling. The Landé g-factors are gg​=2 and ge​=2/3, so a transition from mg​ to me​ shifts by (μB​B/h)(ge​me​−gg​mg​).

Each geometry therefore selects a doublet, with twice the separation in the perpendicular-polarization case. Equal line heights within a pair require equal lower-state populations and an unsaturating probe; line positions do not require that extra population assumption.

Paschen-Back effect

Words: 272 Articles: 3
Zeeman splitting OurBigBook.com
In the Paschen-Back effect, the external magnetic field interaction becomes large compared with the spin-orbit interaction that holds L and S coupled. Then J ceases to be a good approximate quantum number; mL​,mS​ become more useful, with leading electronic shifts ΔE≃μB​B(mL​+gs​mS​). In the ideal complete-decoupling limit an electric-dipole interaction preserves mS​, so its spin contribution cancels between the levels and orbital triplet spacing can reappear. Intermediate fields require mixing the coupled states. This is a change of coupling regime, distinct from the weak-field anomalous Zeeman effect; still larger fields require additional terms beyond this linear model.

Weak spin-forbidden Paschen-Back line (Iweak​∝(β/μB​B)2)

Words: 33
Paschen-Back effect OurBigBook.com
At large but finite magnetic field, opposite-spin admixtures in approximate product eigenstates let nominally spin-forbidden electric-dipole channels borrow intensity. Their amplitudes scale as spin-orbit interaction energy divided by Zeeman energy; their intensities therefore vanish quadratically in that ratio.

Paschen-Back transition-channel count

Paschen-Back effect OurBigBook.com
For a one-electron P-to-S transition with nuclear spin zero, ten electric-dipole sublevel channels have finite strength at weak nonzero field. Six retain finite strength in the complete orbital-spin decoupling limit. Channel count is distinct from spectral frequency count: retaining first-order residual spin-orbit interaction energy gives five distinct frequencies, with two central channels degenerate.

Ion trap

Words: 3k Articles: 25
Atomic measurement methods OurBigBook.com
An ion trap confines an ion using electromagnetic fields, allowing repeated interrogation of the same particle. The name also covers related traps for an electron. A Paul trap uses an oscillating electric quadrupole field; a Penning trap combines a static electric quadrupole field with a static magnetic field. Confinement creates time to measure an energy level, frequency or magnetic dipole moment; it does not itself cool the particle or identify its internal quantum state.
The obstacle is Earnshaw's theorem. In a charge-free neighbourhood the static electric potential Φ obeys Laplace's equation, ∇2Φ=0. For a particle of fixed nonzero electric charge Q, the potential energy QΦ is also a harmonic function. The maximum principle for harmonic functions excludes a strict interior minimum. For a quadratic example, the Hessian matrix has zero trace; it cannot have three positive eigenvalues. A static purely electric field therefore cannot supply three-dimensional stable confinement of a free point electric charge. Time variation in a Paul trap, and the velocity-dependent Lorentz force in a Penning trap, change the assumptions of this argument.

Trapped ion

Words: 33
Ion trap OurBigBook.com
An ion confined by an electromagnetic trap has both internal atomic states and quantized motional modes. Coherent internal-state control, state-dependent fluorescence and resolved-sideband operations allow these degrees of freedom to serve as quantum-information resources.

Trapped-ion quantum control

Words: 2k Articles: 12
Ion trap OurBigBook.com
Trapped-ion quantum control prepares an ion's internal quantum state, couples it to quantized motion with laser pulses, and measures the result through state-dependent fluorescence. Its appeal is access to both a controllable two-level system and a quantum harmonic oscillator in one apparatus.
Confinement, preparation, control and readout solve different problems. The Paul trap's RF electric field confines the ion through its RF-averaged trapping potential; it still produces Paul trap micromotion. Doppler cooling and resolved sideband cooling reduce motional excitation. Optical pumping selects an internal quantum state. A coherent pulse then changes amplitudes, while electron shelving converts an internal population into a detectable stream of photons. A bright/dark count by itself does not reveal a quantum superposition's relative phase; an additional controlled rotation before detection can make that phase affect the measured population.
Trapped-ion quantum computer
Words: 43
Trapped-ion quantum control OurBigBook.com
A quantum processor encoding qubits in long-lived internal states of confined ions. Coherent drives implement single-qubit rotations; shared vibrational modes can mediate entangling gates. Individual fluorescence measurements distinguish bright and dark qubit levels. Mode crowding and residual spin-motion entanglement complicate gates as a single chain grows.
Trapped-ion internal and motional states (∣g,n⟩=∣g⟩⊗∣n⟩)
Words: 992 Articles: 6
Trapped-ion quantum control OurBigBook.com
An internal qubit uses two distinguishable electronic or hyperfine structure quantum states, denoted ∣g⟩,∣e⟩. The ion's centre-of-mass motion has a different Hilbert space. In one approximately harmonic direction, a number state ∣n⟩ has energy En​=ℏν(n+1/2), where ν denotes a motional angular frequency, not ordinary frequency. The tensor product of quantum systems gives ∣g,n⟩. Cooling towards n=0 prepares motion; it does not automatically prepare the internal qubit. Nor does the ground state mean a stationary point particle: zero-point energy and position spread remain.
For several ions, Coulomb forces couple their displacements into collective normal modes. Each selected normal mode has its own quantum harmonic oscillator number states, while each ion retains internal qubit states. A pulse addressing one ion can change a shared mode. This supplies a route to correlations between distant internal quantum states; it also makes residual motional excitation and unwanted excitation of other normal modes relevant. A single-ion pulse calculation alone establishes no experimental multi-ion quantum gate performance.

Harmonic-oscillator recoil matrix element OurBigBook.com
A transition between oscillator energy eigenstates that adds one quantum changes kinetic and potential expectation energies by ℏω/2 each. A sudden unobserved momentum kick instead initially adds its energy only to kinetic motion and leaves the position distribution unchanged. Coherent superpositions distinguish these descriptions. Averaging over motional outcomes gives a recoil-scale total energy; time averaging or dephasing gives equal kinetic and potential shares. A motional sideband is a transition that changes internal excitation and a motional quantum number together. Define the internal energy gap as ℏω0​>0. A carrier drives ∣g,n⟩↔∣e,n⟩; the first red sideband drives ∣g,n⟩↔∣e,n−1⟩; the first blue sideband drives ∣g,n⟩↔∣e,n+1⟩. Their resonant drive angular frequencies follow by subtracting these energy levels. For a Raman transition, the drive is a beam-difference frequency with a sign fixed by the selected internal transition.

Resolved sideband cooling
Words: 248 Articles: 1
Trapped-ion quantum control OurBigBook.com
Resolved sideband cooling removes motional quanta by selectively driving a red motional sideband and then resetting the internal quantum state through spontaneous emission or optical pumping. Spectral resolution requires the effective cooling-transition width smaller than the motional angular frequency in the same units. A narrow Raman transition can meet that requirement even when the optical transition used for Doppler cooling is broad.
The reset is essential: the coherent red motional sideband merely exchanges internal and motional excitation reversibly. To see the distinction, an ideal pulse sends ∣g,1⟩ to −i∣e,0⟩; the same interaction can send it back. An ideal dissipative reset instead takes ∣e,0⟩ to ∣g,0⟩, with information and energy carried into the environment. Repeating this cycle accumulates population near the motional ground state. Recoil during the reset can add motion, and off-resonant excitation can disturb ∣g,0⟩; neither is included in the ideal pulse below.
Raman sideband cooling experiment of 1995

Resolved sideband cooling OurBigBook.com
In 1995, Christopher Monroe and collaborators cooled one 9Be+ ion in a ring/endcap Paul trap. They used 313 nm Doppler cooling and optical pumping into ∣F,mF​⟩=∣2,2⟩. Red-sideband Raman transitions transferred population to ∣1,1⟩, followed by dissipative recycling. Repeating across three directions yielded a reported three-dimensional ground state population of about 92%.[ref]
A variable-frequency Raman transition probe, an exchange pulse and a cycling detection beam converted state populations into fluorescence collected through f/2 optics onto a position-sensitive photomultiplier. Red/blue asymmetry inferred motional occupation; varying probe duration tested the thermal assumption. Off-resonant processes and independently observed heating limited cooling.[ref]
Electron shelving

Trapped-ion quantum control OurBigBook.com
Electron shelving distinguishes an internal quantum state outside a cycling optical transition from one that scatters many photons. In the mercury-ion example in David J. Wineland's lecture, S↔P excitation produces 194 nm fluorescence; transfer to a metastable atomic level D suppresses it. A photomultiplier records bright/dark intervals. Coherent 282 nm interrogation precedes detection to avoid perturbation by the detection beam.[ref]
“Dark” means weak scattering under a particular detection setting. The motional ground state is dark to an ideal red motional sideband for a different reason: there is no lower number state. It can still fluoresce strongly on a cycling detection transition. Shelving's population readout also need not preserve a quantum superposition's quantum coherence; scattered photons carry information about the internal state, and their recoil can disturb motion.

The Paul trap alternates focusing and defocusing electric forces. Their time average along a moving trajectory need not vanish, even when the electric field averages to zero at every fixed point. A Penning trap uses a static electric quadrupole field for axial confinement and a static axial magnetic field for transverse confinement. The Lorentz force bends a moving electric charge's trajectory without doing work. An RF probe may interrogate a trapped particle, but an RF confining voltage is unnecessary in this ideal model. This makes the Penning trap useful for relating cyclotron frequencies and spin precession to a common magnetic field.

Take a single isolated optical transition of angular frequency ω0​. Both beams have laboratory angular frequency ωL​, with laser detuning δ=ωL​−ω0​. Let the pump travel along +z, the probe along −z, v denote an atom's z-velocity, and k=ω0​/c be the approximate vacuum wavenumber; c is the speed of light. To first order in v/c, the laser detunings in the atom's frame are
Δpump​=δ−kv,Δprobe​=δ+kv.
(31)
The pump addresses atoms near v=δ/k, while the probe addresses atoms near v=−δ/k. For the same transition, simultaneous exact resonance requires both expressions to vanish: adding and subtracting gives δ=0 and v=0. The selected atoms can still have substantial transverse velocity. Finite natural linewidth admits a narrow interval of longitudinal velocities; a warm gas has not been cooled.
This is velocity selection, not cancellation of each atom's Doppler shift within a single absorption event. Changing laser detuning selects different atoms for ordinary photon absorption, but only near line centre do these two selected classes overlap. Laser cooling instead changes the distribution of the atoms' velocities through repeated momentum transfer.

Pump-on reduces absorption and raises the detector signal; scanning the laser finds the narrow resonance. Its first application used iodine; pressure and laser jitter limited the resolution.[ref]
For an original detector model, let P0​ be the probe power reaching a photodetector without sample attenuation and let τoff​,τon​ be the sample's probe optical depths. After subtracting a stable detector background, the transmitted powers are
Poff​=P0​e−τoff​,Pon​=P0​e−τon​,Poff​Pon​−Poff​​=eτoff​−τon​−1.
(32)
A positive synchronous change means less probe photon absorption, provided incident probe power is stable and scattered pump light is excluded. For small optical-depth changes the fractional signal is approximately τoff​−τon​. A lock-in amplifier's voltage also depends on gain, reference phase and chopping waveform; it is not automatically this dimensionless ratio.
Useful controls are blocking the pump, detuning far from the feature, reversing or adjusting beam alignment, and repeating the scan at several pump light intensities. Frequency calibration, sample pressure, transit through the beams and laser frequency fluctuations must be assessed separately. Nearly opposed beams leave a residual Doppler shift: for wave vectors k1​,k2​, the simultaneous-resonance condition gives 2δ=(k1​+k2​)⋅v. Exact opposition removes this transverse sensitivity in the first-order model.

In the two-level saturation population model, pe​ and the population-difference reduction q reach half their resonant values at ∣Δ∣=(Γ/2)1+s​. Their half width at half maximum is therefore (Γ/2)1+s​ and their full width at half maximum is Wω​=Γ1+s​ in angular frequency, or Wν​=Wω​/(2π) in hertz. This is power broadening: stronger excitation addresses a wider range of detunings even though the lifetime has not changed.
Increasing s improves the local population-difference reduction q(0)=s/(1+s) but broadens the response. From s=1 to s=9, this reduction increases from 0.5 to 0.9, while the width increases from 2​Γ to 10​Γ. The contrast approaches a limit and the width keeps growing. This single-atom width is not automatically the width of a velocity-averaged pump–probe feature.
For example, if the distribution of velocities is approximately constant across the narrow resonant classes, the population-only overlap integral contains two Lorentzian line shapes: a probe of half width γ=Γ/2 and a pump hole of half width a=γ1+s​. Their centres in kv are separated by 2δ. The convolution of these profiles has half width a+γ in that separation, so its full width at half maximum as a function of δ is a+γ=(Γ/2)(1+1+s​). Even this simplified pump–probe width differs from the single-atom power broadening formula. Finite Doppler broadening and coherent or multilevel effects require further analysis.

Choose a normal distribution with standard deviation σD​ and a weak-probe Lorentzian line shape with half width at half maximum γν​:

Add a deliberately phenomenological Lamb dip:
As​(x)=B(x)−1+4x2/ws2​Cs​​,Cs​=0.241+ss​,ws​=2πΓ​1+s​.
(37)
Here As​ is the absorption coefficient normalized to the pump-off line-centre value. The factor 0.24 is chosen, not inferred from populations or a fit. The dip's assigned full width at half maximum ws​ borrows the single-atom power broadening scale purely to illustrate contrast versus width. It is not the preceding overlap integral or a fit to historical spectra. There are no crossover features in this isolated-transition toy spectrum.
For s=1, the subtracted dip has depth 0.12 and width 8.49 MHz; for s=9, depth 0.216 and width 18.97 MHz. Its half-depth points are x=±ws​/2. Measure that width relative to the curved background B(x), not a horizontal line through the total absorption minimum.
For a chosen cell optical depth τs​(x)=0.4As​(x), the line-centre pump-off transmission is e−0.4≃0.6703. At s=1 it is e−0.352≃0.7033. Crossover resonance (νco​=(νa​+νb​)/2)

Doppler-free saturation spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Two allowed optical transitions sharing a lower quantum state can produce an extra saturation spectroscopy feature even where there is no additional energy level difference. Approximate their wavenumbers by the same k, and let their angular frequencies be ωa​,ωb​. A pump resonant with one transition and an opposed probe resonant with the other satisfy
ωL​−kv=ωa​,ωL​+kv=ωb​,
(38)
so
ωL​=2ωa​+ωb​​,v=2kωb​−ωa​​.
(39)
Exchanging the two transitions selects the opposite velocity. Both beams can then modify the same shared population, producing a crossover near the midpoint. This requires the relevant velocities to be occupied and the transitions to be connected by the population dynamics; not every pair must produce a visible feature. Strength and sign depend on optical pumping and the multilevel structure. Assigning every narrow feature to a separate atomic transition would therefore give false energy levels.
Sodium saturation spectroscopy experiment of 1971
Words: 129
Doppler-free saturation spectroscopy OurBigBook.com
Theodor W. Hänsch, I. S. Shahin and Arthur Leonard Schawlow reported pulsed dye laser saturation spectroscopy of sodium D lines in 1971. They resolved hyperfine structure; delaying the probe revealed persistent changes in ground-level distributions of velocities from optical pumping. Added argon allowed observation of collisional recovery. These measurements probe population memory as well as line positions.[ref]
The two-level saturation population model explains depletion in a closed transition; the delayed multilevel optical pumping signal needs additional populations and time dependence. A measured Doppler-free saturation spectroscopy feature can still contain natural linewidth, power broadening, pressure broadening, finite interaction time, imperfect alignment and laser spectral width. The word “Doppler-free” removes a particular thermal broadening mechanism, not every limit on resolution.
Arthur Leonard Schawlow's 1981 recognition concerned laser spectroscopy.[ref] Theodor W. Hänsch received a distinct award in 2005 for precision laser spectroscopy.[ref]

Optical pumping

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Atomic measurement methods OurBigBook.com
Optical pumping redistributes populations among internal quantum states by selective photon absorption followed by spontaneous emission. It can prepare atoms for measurement and participate in sub-Doppler cooling.
The practical aim is to make otherwise almost equally populated magnetic sublevels behave differently. Repeated absorption and emission can store a population imbalance in the long-lived ground state; a change in photon absorption or fluorescence then reveals a perturbation of that prepared distribution. This combines preparation and measurement: a weak radio wave can reorganize the populations, while abundant optical photons supply the readout.
An imbalance among ground state magnetic sublevels need not be a population inversion between optical energy levels. Optical pumping also supplies excitation in some lasers, where an appropriate population inversion matters for gain. The preparation problem here concerns the distribution within the ground state. A two-level system with only one lower quantum state cannot describe this redistribution.

Optical pumping preparation and readout

Words: 133
Optical pumping OurBigBook.com
Circular polarization selects the sign of the absorbed photon's angular momentum along the beam. Choose that direction as z and define σ+ by the absorption rule m′=m+1, where m is the magnetic quantum number. Spontaneous emission can return an atom to a different magnetic sublevel, so absorption followed by emission is a population-transfer cycle. A sublevel that the chosen beam cannot excite is dark to that beam. Darkness is relative to the selected transition and electromagnetic polarization, rather than a claim that the atom cannot interact with any light.
A static magnetic field along z defines a stable axis and gives Zeeman splitting. A transverse oscillating magnetic field can redistribute magnetic sublevel populations when its frequency matches an allowed splitting. With the appropriate optical transition, that redistribution restores photon absorption: transmitted intensity decreases, or collected fluorescence increases. These are alternative readouts whose detailed sensitivity depends on the transition, viewing direction and electromagnetic polarization.

Kastler-Brossel optical pumping experiments

Words: 265
Optical pumping OurBigBook.com
Alfred Kastler's 1966 lecture recalls his 1950 proposal and distinguishes the early 23Na atomic beam work from later sealed-vapour experiments. Its Fig. 5 shows subsequent sodium radio wave resonances, including multiple-photon transitions.[ref]
The 1952 demonstration by Jean Brossel, Alfred Kastler and Jacques Winter used a sodium atomic beam, lamp light with circular polarization and fluorescence readout. Jean Brossel was a central experimental contributor; Alfred Kastler received the 1966 Nobel Prize in Physics alone.[ref][ref]
The lecture also describes a 199Hg experiment: a pumping beam with circular polarization prepares the vapour, while a perpendicular probe converts transverse magnetic dipole moment Larmor precession into modulated absorption at a photodetector. Interrupting pump and RF together exposes decaying free Larmor precession. Its envelope measures transverse relaxation under that model; it is distinct from the sodium atomic beam fluorescence signal.[ref]
MIT's later rubidium experiment pumps natural 85Rb/87Rb with a discharge lamp filtered to D1 (5S1/2​→5P1/2​, near 795 nm). A polarizer and quarter-wave plate precede a heated rubidium/neon cell. Helmholtz coils set a weak static magnetic field. Separate transverse RF mixing increases absorption, measured by photodiode transmission.[ref]
Compare resonant and detuned RF with the optical beam fixed, then change the calibrated static magnetic field: a true magnetic sublevel resonance should move with its Zeeman splitting. Lamp drift, stray magnetic fields, imperfect circular polarization, optical attenuation and RF power broadening can change the observed signal. Consequently, a transmission dip alone does not determine every sublevel population. These are measurement-design considerations, not additional reported historical observations.

Three-sublevel optical pumping model (F=1→F′=0)

Words: 375
Optical pumping OurBigBook.com
Consider an original hypothetical atom with a lower angular momentum multiplet F=1, m=−1,0,+1, and one opposite-parity excited level F′=0,m′=0. Stipulate that all spontaneous emission returns to these three lower quantum states, with no other decay channel. This is an isolated four-state model, not the actual sodium or rubidium D-line structure. In particular, the physical rubidium cell above contains multiple hyperfine structure levels.
The electric-dipole selection rule permits ΔF=−1 here; σ+ absorption with Δm=+1 excites only m=−1. Decay from F′=0 has three equal integrated branching probabilities b−​=b0​=b+​=1/3: rotational symmetry gives equal squared Clebsch-Gordan coefficients. The emitted photons carry the three permitted angular momentum projections; equal integrated branching does not imply equal intensity in every observation direction. Thus m=0 and m=+1 are both dark. The chosen beam cannot prepare a unique pure m=+1 state.
Let R≥0 be the absorption rate of an atom in m=−1, and let Γ be the excited-state spontaneous emission rate, both in inverse seconds. Assume R,γ≪Γ, negligible stimulated emission, and no maintained quantum coherence between sublevels. Eliminating the short-lived excited population gives normalized lower populations p−​+p0​+p+​=1 to this approximation. At each scattering event the atom leaves m=−1 with probability 2/3; the remaining 1/3 simply returns it there.
Model depolarizing collisions and other population relaxation by resets to the unpolarized distribution at rate γ≥0. The rate equations are
p˙​−​=−32R​p−​+γ(31​−p−​),p˙​0​=3R​p−​+γ(31​−p0​),p˙​+​=3R​p−​+γ(31​−p+​).
(40)
This relaxation prescription assumes that Zeeman splitting is small compared with thermal energy, so the unpolarized distribution approximates thermal equilibrium. It is not an energy-independent relaxation law at arbitrarily low temperature.
Every transfer has a nonnegative rate: optical transfers −→0 and −→+ each have rate R/3, and relaxation transfers between each distinct pair have rate γ/3. These define a continuous-time Markov chain. The three derivatives sum to zero, and at pi​=0 the corresponding derivative cannot be negative. Hence the model conserves population and preserves nonnegative populations. Optical cycles that return to m=−1 contribute to scattering even though they cause no net population transfer.

p−∗​=3γ+2Rγ​,p0∗​=p+∗​=3γ+2Rγ+R​,⟨m⟩∗=p+∗​−p−∗​=3γ+2RR​.
(41)
The nonzero mean magnetic quantum number represents atomic orientation. Increasing R/γ empties the bright state, but leaves two dark populations. For R=0, relaxation alone gives pi​(t)=1/3+[pi​(0)−1/3]e−γt. When γ=0 and R>0, every distribution with p−​=0 is stationary; the initial difference between the two dark populations survives. The equal dark populations below follow from the specified unpolarized initial condition.
Starting from pi​(0)=1/3, the solution for R>0 or γ>0 is
p−​(t)=p−∗​+(31​−p−∗​)e−(γ+2R/3)t,p0​(t)=p+​(t)=21−p−​(t)​.
(42)
For pure pumping, take p−∗​=0 in this formula. Its redistribution time is 3/(2R), longer than the mean scattering interval 1/R of a bright atom, because one third of scattering events return it to the same sublevel. For arbitrary initial populations the additional mode satisfies p0​(t)−p+​(t)=[p0​(0)−p+​(0)]e−γt.
For an original numerical example choose R=6 s−1 and γ=1 s−1, with Γ much larger than either. Then
(p−∗​,p0∗​,p+∗​)=151​(1,7,7),⟨m⟩∗=52​,τpump​=γ+2R/31​=0.20 s.
(43)
At t=τpump​, p−​≃0.1648, while p0​=p+​≃0.4176. If the light is then switched off, relaxation returns all three populations toward 1/3 with time constant 1/γ=1 s. Faster optical preparation and slower dark recovery measure different combinations of rates.
In an optically thin uniform sample of N atoms, with equal collection efficiency η for each decay branch, the detected fluorescence count rate is approximately Sfl​=ηNRp−​. The same scattering removes pump photons, giving Φout​≃Φin​−NRp−​ when depletion is small. For the chosen example the steady scattering rate is R/15=0.40 s−1 per atom, compared with the initial R/3=2 s−1. Pumping lowers this signal fivefold, while increasing transmission. If rapid mixing restores nearly uniform populations, scattering rises again. Reabsorption, strong attenuation, unequal collection efficiencies or coherent RF dynamics require a more detailed model; the reset rate γ does not stand for an exact RF Hamiltonian.

Laser cooling

Words: 3k Articles: 15
Atomic measurement methods OurBigBook.com
Laser cooling uses laser light to reduce the random velocities of chemical atoms, and therefore their translational temperature. The striking ingredient is selective photon absorption: an atom moving towards a beam sees a Doppler shift that can make it absorb more strongly. Each absorbed photon transfers momentum along the beam; repeated absorption and spontaneous emission can then remove kinetic energy. Doppler cooling makes this selection with the atom's motion, while sub-Doppler cooling also exploits its internal quantum states.
Cooling makes chemical atoms move slowly enough for longer interrogation in atomic clocks and atom interferometry, and easier loading into an optical trap. The same radiation pressure that pushes an atom can cool it: with suitably tuned opposing beams, whichever direction the atom moves, it receives the stronger push against that motion.

Doppler cooling

Words: 733 Articles: 2
Laser cooling OurBigBook.com
Consider equal opposing laser beams along the x axis and an atom with velocity v. Let ωL​ be their angular frequency, ω0​ the atomic resonance angular frequency, k=2π/λ>0 their wavenumber, and δ=ωL​−ω0​ the laser detuning. Red detuning means δ<0. To first order in v/c, the atom sees
ω+′​=ωL​−kv,ω−′​=ωL​+kv,δ+​=δ−kv,δ−​=δ+kv.
(44)
For small positive v, the beam travelling towards negative x is closer to resonance and causes more photon absorption; its momentum kicks point against v. The beam travelling towards positive x is further from resonance. Reversing v exchanges the roles of the two beams. This is a Doppler effect on the absorption rates, rather than a need to follow each atom with a moving beam.
An absorbed photon gives the atom momentum ±ℏk, where ℏ=h/(2π) is the reduced Planck constant. Subsequent spontaneous emission gives a recoil opposite to the emitted photon. For an emission pattern symmetric under reversal of direction, that recoil has zero expected value, but nonzero variance. Its mean therefore leaves the directional absorption force intact, while its randomness adds recoil energy. Random absorption times and choices of beam add further momentum fluctuations. Zero mean recoil does not mean zero heating.
Doppler cooling force (f(v)≃−αv)

Doppler cooling OurBigBook.com
Use a closed two-level system with spontaneous emission population decay Pe​(t)=Pe​(0)e−Γt. Here Γ is a decay rate in inverse seconds and also the full width at half maximum of the natural linewidth expressed in angular frequency. The corresponding full width in hertz is Γ/(2π); the angular half width is Γ/2. These conventions determine every factor of two and 2π below.
Let s be the on-resonance saturation parameter of each beam, with total excitation weak enough that saturation and coherent coupling between beams can be neglected. The independent-beam scattering rates and net force are
R±​(v)=2Γs​1+4(δ∓kv)2/Γ21​,f(v)=ℏk(R+​(v)−R−​(v)).
(45)
The force is the photon momentum per absorption multiplied by the difference in absorption rates. With dimensionless laser detuning d=δ/Γ and dimensionless velocity u=kv/Γ, write
f(v)=2ℏkΓs​F(u),F(u)=1+4(d−u)21​−1+4(d+u)21​.
(46)
For the example d=−0.5 and u=0.25, the positive and negative beam factors are respectively 4/13 and 4/5. Thus F(0.25)=−32/65≃−0.4923: the atom is moving right and the net force points left. All values in this example are dimensionless.
Subtracting the two fractions gives an especially useful sign check:
F(u)=(1+4(d−u)2)(1+4(d+u)2)16du​,F′(0)=(1+4d2)216d​.
(47)
For red detuning, the force opposes nonzero v throughout this ideal model; its useful magnitude eventually falls at large ∣u∣. Near zero, a Taylor series gives damping
f(v)=−αv+O(v3),α=−(1+4d2)28ℏk2sd​>0.
(48)
At d=−0.5, F′(0)=−2 and α=ℏk2s. For blue detuning the sign reverses and the small-velocity motion is amplified; at exact resonance the opposing mean forces cancel in this symmetric model. Its derivation assumes weak excitation, a closed two-level system, equal beam intensities and nonrelativistic velocities; real multilevel atoms need additional physics.
Doppler cooling limit (TD​=ℏΓ/(2kB​))
Words: 213
Doppler cooling OurBigBook.com
Damping removes random kinetic energy, but the discrete photon kicks cause diffusion in momentum. Their balance gives a nonzero temperature. Define the momentum diffusion coefficient Dp​ by the noise contribution d⟨px2​⟩/dt=2Dp​. With atom mass m and linear damping coefficient α,
dtd⟨px2​⟩​=−m2α​⟨px2​⟩+2Dp​,kB​T=m⟨px2​⟩​=αDp​​
(49)
at stationary balance, where kB​ is the Boltzmann constant and mean momentum is zero.
For ideal three-dimensional optical molasses with three identical independent beam pairs and isotropic spontaneous emission, the x-pair absorption rate at rest is Rx​=Γs/(1+4d2). Absorption from that pair contributes (ℏk)2Rx​ to the noise growth of ⟨px2​⟩. Emission from all three pairs contributes the same amount: its total rate is 3Rx​ and each emitted photon has mean squared x-momentum (ℏk)2/3. Hence Dp​=(ℏk)2Rx​. Using the Doppler cooling force coefficient gives
T(d)=8kB​ℏΓ​−d1+4d2​,d<0.
(50)
Put a=−d>0. Then (1+4d2)/(−d)=a−1+4a≥4, with equality at a=1/2. The ideal weak-field Doppler cooling limit is therefore TD​=ℏΓ/(2kB​) at δ=−Γ/2. It is the minimum of this specified diffusion-and-damping model, rather than a universal lower bound for laser cooling. The diffusion approximation also assumes recoil energy much smaller than ℏΓ. In a one-pair geometry, emission patterns and transverse recoil change the diffusion bookkeeping. [ref].

Optical molasses

Words: 316 Articles: 1
Laser cooling OurBigBook.com
Optical molasses surrounds slow chemical atoms with opposing red-detuned laser beams, usually three pairs along perpendicular axes. In the elementary Doppler cooling picture, each pair damps one component of velocity. The result resembles viscous drag, even though the atoms are moving through a vacuum rather than a liquid.
Uniform balanced optical molasses supplies velocity damping, without a restoring force towards a chosen position. An atom at rest has zero mean force wherever it sits within the uniform illuminated region. Without noise or external forces, mv˙=−αv gives
v(t)=v0​e−αt/m,x(t)=x0​+αmv0​​(1−e−αt/m).
(51)
The atom approaches a position determined by its initial condition, not the beam intersection. Recoil-driven diffusion and gravity eventually remove atoms from finite beams. A long residence time in optical molasses is therefore compatible with the absence of position trapping. An optical trap provides spatial confinement by a different force mechanism; a magneto-optical trap adds a position-dependent magnetic field and suitable beam electromagnetic polarization to create a restoring force.
Optical molasses experiment of 1985
Words: 181
Optical molasses OurBigBook.com
Steven Chu's Bell Laboratories team prepared sodium atoms by pulsed-laser evaporation of a pellet. A frequency-swept opposing beam slowed them before six crossed laser beams supplied optical molasses. The vacuum chamber used a shield coated with graphite and cooled with liquid nitrogen as a pump. Fluorescence provided the readout; the initial beams were aligned as closely counterpropagating as possible. [ref].
After equilibration, the team switched off the cooling light for a variable interval, then restored it. Faster atoms escaped during the dark interval; slower atoms were recaptured. The recaptured fraction versus delay constrained the velocity distribution and hence temperature. The inference depended on the initial cloud shape and recapture volume: Steven Chu later acknowledged adjusting a geometry correction towards the expected Doppler cooling limit. Delay was the scanned variable, and the cooling beams themselves supplied the release/recapture control; visible fluorescence alone could not establish temperature. [ref].

Sub-Doppler cooling

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Laser cooling OurBigBook.com
Real atoms have multiple internal quantum states. Optical pumping and spatially varying electromagnetic polarization can remove kinetic energy by additional mechanisms, producing sub-Doppler cooling below the ideal Doppler cooling limit. In polarization-gradient cooling, state-dependent energy shifts from the Stark effect and delayed optical pumping make atoms repeatedly climb potential energy hills. This mechanism needs the internal-state structure omitted by the independent-beam two-level system above. [ref].
William D. Phillips's team tested unexpectedly cold sodium molasses with time-of-flight atom detection. A probe above the cloud initially saw no atoms; deliberately heating them verified that the detector worked. Moving the probe below the cloud produced arrival signals consistent with temperatures below the Doppler cooling limit. Independent release/recapture checks used sharply apertured beams and included gravity; uncertain cloud and probe geometry still limited the inferred temperature. These controls tested the thermometer as well as the cooling theory. [ref].
Sub-Doppler cooling discovery thermometry
Words: 155
Sub-Doppler cooling OurBigBook.com
The 1988 experiment loaded sodium optical molasses from a slowed atomic beam. After stopping loading, a shutter extinguished the six cooling beams. Released atoms crossed a lower probe; a photomultiplier recorded fluorescence versus arrival time. Calculations integrated the measured initial cloud distribution and an assumed three-dimensional Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, including gravity and detection geometry. The minimum was 43±20 μK, versus the 240 μK Doppler cooling limit.[ref]
Probe separation, probe intensity, cloud density and shutter timing were varied. Fountain-height, horizontal-spreading and release/recapture measurements also gave below-limit results. Geometry remained an uncertainty; agreement among complementary thermometers made a detector artifact less plausible. These measured released atoms, rather than an in-situ velocity distribution.[ref]
Steven Chu's account connects the explanation to optical pumping, Stark effect shifts and spatially changing electromagnetic polarization; Claude Cohen-Tannoudji's lecture separates this mechanism from subrecoil schemes. Their lectures and William D. Phillips's describe complementary experimental and theoretical routes.[ref][ref]

A spatial image after a chosen dark interval is a different readout from continuously recording arrivals at a fixed probe. Here is an original idealised fluorescence imaging model: release a dilute cloud, let it move freely, then apply a short uniform probe pulse. Neglect collisions, residual forces, attenuation and motion during the pulse. Use each image's cloud centre to remove mean drift. Uniform gravity shifts that centre without changing the centred variance.
For each atom let x(t)=x0​+v0​t along a horizontal imaging axis. Expanding the square about the expected values gives exactly
σx2​(t)=σx02​+2Cxv​t+σv2​t2,Cxv​=Cov(x0​,v0​).
(52)
No Gaussian distribution is needed for this variance identity. A jointly Gaussian distribution of initial positions and velocities does make the later density Gaussian. For a separable three-dimensional cloud viewed along z, integration along the viewing direction gives the column density
ncol​(x,y;t)=∫n(x,y,z;t)dz=2πσx​(t)σy​(t)N​exp[−2σx2​(t)(x−xˉ(t))2​−2σy2​(t)(y−yˉ​(t))2​].
(53)
Here N is atom number. Integrating this image along y leaves a one-dimensional Gaussian distribution with standard deviation σx​(t). This is a projected density measurement, not a three-dimensional radius or a direct velocity histogram. Under the uniform, optically thin probe assumptions, expected fluorescence is proportional to this column density. A known, independent point spread function with finite variance adds its own variance to the measured width; probe duration and intensity gradients need separate treatment.
For a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, Tx​=mσv2​/kB​, where m is atomic mass and kB​ the Boltzmann constant. For a nonthermal distribution this defines a directional second-moment temperature, which need not describe every feature of the distribution. A covariance between position and velocity can initially narrow the cloud even though σv2​ is positive. The physical covariance matrix requires Cxv2​≤σx02​σv2​.
Choose σx0​=0.60 mm, σv​=0.060 ms−1 and Cxv​=−0.018 mm2ms−1, giving correlation coefficient −1/2. With t in milliseconds, the numerical variance in square millimetres is 0.36−0.036t+0.0036t2. Its minimum occurs at 5 ms, with standard deviation 0.27​ mm. These chosen values satisfy the covariance matrix constraint; early contraction is compatible with free motion.
Generate thirteen synthetic variance observations at equally spaced times from 0 to 30 ms, adding independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.012 mm2. Linear least squares fits all three coefficients in a+bt+ct2. The example yields a≃0.37026 mm2, b≃−0.036413 mm2ms−1 and c≃0.0035820 mm2ms−2. With the chosen approximate sodium mass m=3.82×10−26 kg, the true Tx​ is 9.96 μK and the fitted value is 9.91 μK. This is a fit to generated width data, not historical observations.
If the same data are fitted to a+ct2, forcing Cxv​=0, the inferred Tx​ falls to 6.79 μK. The omitted term is partly absorbed into both fitted coefficients. In noiseless linear least squares with a free intercept, its precise effect on the quadratic coefficient is
cforced​=σv2​+2Cxv​Vart​(t2)Covt​(t2,t)​,
(54)
where the subscript denotes equal-weight moments over the chosen observation times, using one consistent unit system. Finite optical pumping time lets an atom climb a light-shift hill before transfer into a lower magnetic sublevel. Spontaneous emission dissipates the gained potential energy; climbing alone is conservative.[ref]
To make the geometry and signs explicit, take an original choice of phase origin for equal opposing waves:
E(z)=E0​(x^eikz+iy^​e−ikz),k=λ2π​,ϵ±​=2​x^±iy^​​,w±​(z)=21±cos(2kz)​.
(55)
The real electric field is Re[E(z)e−iωL​t]; λ is wavelength. The fractions w±​ are squared projections onto the defined circular basis vectors, divided by total intensity. Their sum is one: interference changes electromagnetic polarization despite constant total intensity. At z=0,λ/4,λ/2 the field is respectively ϵ+​,ϵ−​,ϵ+​; halfway between these positions it is linearly polarized. Specifying the vectors avoids an observer-dependent verbal handedness convention.
For an illustrative Jg​=1/2→Je​=3/2 angular momentum transition, use the squared Clebsch-Gordan coefficients 1 and 1/3 for the strong and weak circular couplings from each lower magnetic sublevel. Interchanging circular components interchanges these strengths. The weighted sums are w+​+w−​/3=(2+cos(2kz))/3 and w−​+w+​/3=(2−cos(2kz))/3. Rescaling their common negative shift gives
U+​(z)=−U0​−2U0​​cos(2kz),U−​(z)=−U0​+2U0​​cos(2kz),U0​>0.
(56)
Both potential energies are negative relative to the unilluminated level. Each hill has height U0​, and opposite hills are displaced by λ/4. An atom starting at the U+​ minimum at z=0 loses U0​ of kinetic energy if it reaches z=λ/4 on that branch. A pump transfer there lowers its potential energy by U0​, leaving it at a U−​ minimum. The next uphill segment ends at z=λ/2, where the favoured transfer is reversed. Actual transfers are stochastic and need not occur exactly at these extrema.
For one completed climb and pump, conservation of energy gives ΔK=−U0​, while the ground-state potential energy returns to its starting value. Neglecting recoil and treating the scattered photon as the sole outgoing radiation change, ℏ(ωout​−ωL​)=U0​. A potential drop is an internal-state reset, not an automatic equal upward kick in kinetic energy. Random emission nevertheless adds momentum fluctuations and recoil energy, so useful cooling requires the dissipated energy to compete with that heating.
The recoil energy ER​=(ℏk)2/(2m) sets a different scale from kB​TD​=ℏΓ/2. Conventional Sisyphus cooling reaches the recoil regime when reducing the hill height also weakens cooling; it is not a claim of arbitrarily small temperature at vanishing intensity. Subrecoil techniques need further physics.[ref]

As a hypothetical design, take vi​=300 ms−1, vf​=30 ms−1 and a=5.0×104 ms−2. The required length is 0.891 m and flight time (vi​−vf​)/a=5.4 ms. When EF​>0, the outer contour belongs to the lower branch and the inner one to the upper branch. In the Maxwellian approximation used here, qji​=8.6×10−12Ωji​/(gj​Te​​) in m3s−1, and detailed balance fixes the excitation coefficient. Its value and temperature dependence encode atomic scattering physics beyond the elementary Boltzmann factor.

For a normalized electron speed distribution fT​(v), the atomic transition rate coefficient is qij​(T)=∫σij​(v)vfT​(v)dv. Its dimensions are volume per time, so the rate per target atom is ne​qij​. Maxwellian detailed balance gives qji​=(gi​/gj​)e(Ej​−Ei​)/kTqij​ for Ej​>Ei​.

Atomic physics OurBigBook.com

Delta electron

Words: 23
Ionization OurBigBook.com
An energetic secondary electron knocked out by a charged particle. It can radiate above a Cherenkov radiation threshold even when the primary particle is below threshold.

Ionization continuum

Words: 41
Ionization OurBigBook.com
The continuous set of scattering states consisting of a residual ion and a free electron, beginning at the relevant ionization threshold. A bound Rydberg series approaches this threshold; the continuum is a set of states rather than the act of ionization.

Ionization fraction (x=ne​/(nH​+ne​))

Words: 25
Ionization OurBigBook.com
The fraction of nuclei in a specified ionized state. For pure singly ionized hydrogen, x=ne​/(nH​+ne​) by charge neutrality; a different species or normalization requires a different definition.

Degree of ionization (α=Nion​/Nnuclei​)

Words: 37
Ionization OurBigBook.com
The fraction of a specified population of chemical atoms that has become ionized. For singly ionized atoms with no external charge source, charge neutrality gives equal free-electron and ion number densities. Its equilibrium value depends on both temperature and total number density through the Saha ionization equation.

Tunnel ionization

Words: 7
Ionization OurBigBook.com
Tunnel ionization is ionization through quantum tunnelling across a field-distorted binding barrier.

Electron avalanche

Words: 12
Ionization OurBigBook.com
An ionization cascade in which electrons accelerated by an electric field produce further free electrons through collisional ionization.

Three-body recombination

Words: 50
Ionization OurBigBook.com
Three-body recombination captures an electron while a second free electron carries away energy, the inverse of direct electron-impact ionization. Its rate scales as the parent-ion density times the square of electron density. It is usually negligible compared with two-body radiative recombination and dielectronic recombination in the low-density solar corona, but matters in sufficiently dense plasmas.

Dielectronic recombination

Words: 229 Articles: 3
Ionization OurBigBook.com
A free electron is resonantly captured while exciting the ionic core, producing a doubly excited state above the parent-ion threshold. Capture becomes permanent recombination only if the state undergoes radiative stabilization rather than autoionization. For resonance d, entrance ion i, and Maxwellian electrons, αd​=(gd​/(2gi​))(h2/(2πmkT))3/2e−Ed​/kTAdia​Astabr​/(Atota​+Atotr​). Detailed balance determines the capture rate; a steady population balance determines the survival factor. The rate coefficient has dimensions volume per time.

Resonance-temperature dependence of dielectronic recombination (αd​(T)∝T−3/2e−Ed​/kT)

Words: 47
Dielectronic recombination OurBigBook.com
For temperature-independent atomic rates and an isolated positive-energy resonance, dielectronic recombination has the displayed dependence. Differentiating its logarithm gives a maximum at kT=2Ed​/3. A sum of resonances can have several peaks, and near-threshold resonances change the low-temperature behavior. Collisional destruction of captured high levels can introduce density dependence.

Radiative stabilization

Words: 57
Dielectronic recombination OurBigBook.com
Radiative stabilization occurs when a photon emission from an autoionizing state leads to a bound state, preventing electron re-ejection. For one radiative channel and one autoionization channel, its probability is Ar​/(Aa​+Ar​). With several channels, use summed losses and the total rate of successful stabilizing decays; a cascade through another autoionizing state requires its eventual survival probability.

Dielectronic capture

Words: 55
Dielectronic recombination OurBigBook.com
Dielectronic capture is the resonant capture stage inverse to a specified autoionization channel. For an entrance ion of weight gi​ and resonance of weight gd​ and energy Ed​>0, its Maxwellian coefficient is Cd​=(gd​/(2gi​))(h2/(2πmkT))3/2e−Ed​/kTAdia​. This follows by equating capture and autoionization fluxes at thermodynamic equilibrium. Capture alone need not produce a permanently recombined ion.

Autoionization

Words: 40
Ionization OurBigBook.com
An excited atom or ion above an electron-emission threshold can decay without a photon by ejecting an electron and leaving a more highly charged ion. This is autoionization. Its rate competes with radiative stabilization in dielectronic recombination; the inverse electron-capture channel is dielectronic capture.

Photoionization (hν≥Ebind​)

Words: 279 Articles: 5
Ionization OurBigBook.com
Photoionization removes a bound electron when an atom or ion absorbs a sufficiently energetic photon. The threshold is its ionization energy. The excess photon energy becomes kinetic energy of the products; subsequent collisions can heat the gas or cause secondary ionizations. A photoionization rate and a photoionization equilibrium are distinct concepts: equilibrium also requires specified recombination and other reaction rates.

Ionization parameter (U=QH​/(4πr2nH​c))

Words: 53
Photoionization OurBigBook.com
The ionization parameter compares the local density of hydrogen-ionizing photons with the hydrogen number density. For an unattenuated isotropic source the displayed form uses its ionizing photon production rate QH​. Ionic fractions depend on U together with the radiation spectrum, temperature, recombination rates and shielding, so U alone does not determine every emission-line ratio.

Photoelectron

Words: 21
Photoionization OurBigBook.com
An electron ejected following photon absorption. For a free residual ion with negligible recoil, the emitted electron's kinetic energy equals incident photon energy minus the ionization binding energy.

Photoionization OurBigBook.com
For isotropic specific intensity Jν​, absorption cross-section σν​, and threshold frequency ν0​, the photoionization rate per target atom is
Γ=4π∫ν0​∞​hνJν​σν​​dν.
(63)
For a directed incident flux, replace 4πJν​ by its spectral flux density. The factor hν converts energy flux into photon flux. This rate alone does not imply photoionization equilibrium.
