Words: 61
Photoionization rate OurBigBook.com
At an unattenuated inner boundary, define photon-weighted cross section moments ⟨σk⟩=Q−1∫σνk​Lν​/(hν)dν. Across a layer dr, the inverse-square geometrical factor contributes −2dr/r, and expanding e−nH​(1−ζ)σν​dr contributes −nH​(1−ζ)dr⟨σ2⟩/⟨σ⟩. Both are first order; a plane-parallel treatment can suppress the former only as a separate geometrical approximation. The second moment occurs because the photoionization rate weights an already attenuated spectrum by another cross section.

Photoionization heating

Words: 41
Photoionization OurBigBook.com
Absorption of an ionizing photon leaves energy in a photoelectron above the binding energy. Thermalization supplies heat to the gas. Photoionization heating competes with the astrophysical cooling function, can establish thermal equilibrium, and can raise the pressure enough to inhibit baryon accretion into shallow dark-matter haloes.

Radiative recombination (A++e−→A+γ)

Words: 189 Articles: 4
Ionization OurBigBook.com
A free electron can be captured by an ion while a photon carries away binding and kinetic energy. This radiative recombination process contributes free-bound radiation to plasma cooling and balances collisional ionization in a collisional-equilibrium plasma.

Recombination cooling of ionized hydrogen

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Radiative recombination OurBigBook.com
Radiative recombination removes the kinetic energy of captured electrons from a plasma. The thermal cooling per event is not the entire emitted photon energy: binding energy had been stored as ionization energy. If recombination is the only cooling and ionization is balanced, the mean removed kinetic energy equals the mean photoelectron heating energy.
Recombination-weighted electron energy (⟨E⟩rec​)
Words: 35
Recombination cooling of ionized hydrogen OurBigBook.com
The mean kinetic energy removed per recombination is ⟨E⟩rec​=∫EfT​(E)σrec​(E)v(E)dE/∫fT​(E)σrec​(E)v(E)dE. The capture-rate weighting generally differs from averaging an unselected Maxwell distribution, so ⟨E⟩rec​=3kB​T/2 is only an additional approximation.

Recombination line

Words: 31
Radiative recombination OurBigBook.com
A recombination line is a spectral line produced after a free electron is captured, often through a subsequent radiative cascade among bound levels. Its emissivity is computed with an effective recombination coefficient, distinct from the free-bound recombination continuum.

Effective recombination coefficient (αℓeff​)

Words: 52
Radiative recombination OurBigBook.com
The effective recombination coefficient for a spectral line counts recombinations and subsequent radiative cascades producing that line. At sufficiently low density, its photon production rate per volume is ne​nparent​αℓeff​. It depends on gas temperature, optical-depth assumptions such as Case B recombination, and sometimes density. It differs from the total rate coefficient removing the parent ion.

Collisional ionization (A+e−→A++2e−)

Words: 172 Articles: 3
Ionization OurBigBook.com
In collisional ionization, an energetic collision frees a bound electron. The process consumes kinetic energy and changes the electron and ion populations controlling plasma cooling. In a thermal gas its rate competes with recombination and depends strongly on the ionization threshold relative to temperature.

Excitation-autoionization

Words: 32
Collisional ionization OurBigBook.com
Electron impact can excite an ion into a state above an electron-emission threshold, which then ejects a bound electron by autoionization. This two-stage excitation-autoionization contributes to collisional ionization in addition to direct impact removal.

Collisional ionization equilibrium (ni​Ci​(T)=ni+1​αi+1​(T))

Words: 99 Articles: 1
Collisional ionization OurBigBook.com
In collisional ionization equilibrium, collision-driven ionization and recombination balance for the populated ion stages, determining their relative abundances at a given temperature. The resulting cooling curve includes the loss of line-emitting bound states as temperature increases. Rapidly cooling gas or external photoionization can invalidate this equilibrium assumption.
Coronal approximation
Words: 55
Collisional ionization equilibrium OurBigBook.com
The coronal approximation treats an optically thin, low-density plasma with electron-impact ionization balanced by radiative and dielectronic recombination. Excited-level populations are determined mainly by collisional excitation and radiative decay, not by a Boltzmann distribution over levels. Ion fractions can depend primarily on electron temperature while metastable populations retain density dependence; this distinction enables density diagnostics.

Absorption imaging

Words: 26
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
Determining the column density of a cloud of chemical atoms from the attenuation of a probe beam of light; the measured image integrates through the cloud along the viewing direction.

Electronic transition

Words: 281 Articles: 7
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
A change between electronic energy eigenstates of a chemical atom or another system.

Photon absorption recoil correction (hν=ΔE+ΔE2/(2Mc2))

Electronic transition OurBigBook.com
An initially stationary isolated chemical atom of rest mass M absorbing a single photon must recoil. If the internal excitation changes its rest mass by ΔM=ΔE/c2, conservation of energy and conservation of momentum give Mc2+hν=(Mc2+ΔE)2+(hν)2​ and hence the exact formula in the title. The additional positive energy supplies recoil. An external body sharing the momentum, or an initially moving chemical atom, changes this laboratory resonance condition.

Deslandres table

Words: 32
Electronic transition OurBigBook.com
A two-index arrangement of vibronic transition wavenumbers. Differences along rows isolate lower-state spacings; differences down columns isolate upper-state spacings. Deviations from exact separability can expose measurement uncertainty, rotational structure or incorrect assignments.

Vibrational progression

Words: 29
Electronic transition OurBigBook.com
A sequence of vibronic transitions sharing a lower vibrational level and reaching successive vibrational levels of another electronic state. frequency differences remove the common electronic origin and reveal vibrational spacings.

Words: 156 Articles: 3
Electronic transition OurBigBook.com
Electronic excitation occurs rapidly compared with nuclear motion. In the Condon approximation, vibronic intensities are proportional to squared overlaps of initial and final vibrational wavefunctions; vertical arrows on a potential diagram summarize this overlap rather than a nuclear trajectory.

Franck-Condon factor (∣⟨χv′​∣χv′′​⟩∣2)

Words: 117 Articles: 2
Franck-Condon principle OurBigBook.com
The squared vibrational overlap ∣⟨χv′​∣χv′′​⟩∣2 entering a vibronic intensity when the electronic transition moment is treated as constant over nuclear coordinates.
Displaced-oscillator Franck-Condon progression (Iν​∝e−SSν/ν!)
Words: 96 Articles: 1
Franck-Condon factor OurBigBook.com
For equal-frequency harmonic ground and excited molecular potentials displaced by ΔQ, the low-temperature vibrational overlap has the Poisson weights in the title, with S=Mωv​(ΔQ)2/(2ℏ). Optical lines occur at E00​+νℏωv​, apart from broadening and slowly varying electronic or optical prefactors. The normalized weights sum to one and have mean vibrational excitation S. Unequal frequencies, several vibrations, hot initial states and intermolecular coupling modify this simple Franck-Condon principle model.
Huang-Rhys factor (S=Mωv​(ΔQ)2/(2ℏ))
Words: 25
Displaced-oscillator Franck-Condon progression OurBigBook.com
The dimensionless displacement strength for the equal-frequency single-vibration model in displaced-oscillator Franck-Condon progression. It equals the mean number of excited vibrational quanta in its zero-temperature overlap distribution.

Geiger-Marsden experiment

Words: 291 Articles: 1
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com
The Geiger-Marsden experiment probes the interior of a chemical atom by counting alpha particles deflected by metal foils. The surprising observation was a small population returning towards the incident side. Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden performed the experiments under Ernest Rutherford's direction; Ernest Rutherford developed the Rutherford model in 1911. Observation and interpretation were distinct contributions.[ref]
In 1909, a radon source and its radioactive decay products in a conical glass tube supplied alpha particles through a mica window towards a reflector. Lead shielded a fixed zinc sulfide screen from direct hits; an optical microscope resolved individual particle scintillations. Reflectors occupied the same position. Reflector-out counts tested air scattering; stacked gold foils and bare glass tested thickness and support contributions.[ref]
Nearby source geometry blurred incidence angles. Extrapolating platinum counts uniformly over a hemisphere was an assumption, not a universal reflection probability.[ref]

Geiger-Marsden angular-scattering experiment of 1913

Words: 139
Geiger-Marsden experiment OurBigBook.com
The later angular test used an evacuated chamber with a radon source and scattering foil fixed in place. A diaphragm served as a collimator; a zinc sulfide screen and attached optical microscope rotated about the foil on a graduated platform. Particle scintillation counts sampled successive angles. Foil-out counts supplied background subtraction, with corrections for source radioactive decay and finite beam width. Shielding reduced interfering radiation, but screen glow limited large angles. This tested the Rutherford differential cross-section.[ref]

Rutherford scattering

Words: 973 Articles: 6
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com Tags: Atomic nucleus
Rutherford scattering is elastic scattering by a Coulomb potential. In the repulsive classical case, a positively charged projectile bends around a positively charged atomic nucleus. A close approach can turn it backwards without a contact collision. The calculation connects an invisible impact parameter with a measurable outgoing angle, then with a differential scattering cross-section and a detector count.
Assume a projectile of mass m and electric charge ze, a stationary point atomic nucleus of electric charge Ze, and positive z,Z. Here e is the elementary charge. Neglect nuclear recoil, electron screening effect, energy loss, and the nuclear force. With vacuum permittivity ε0​, define
V(r)=rκ​,κ=4πε0​zZe2​>0,E=21​mv2,L=mvb.
(64)
Here E and v are the incident kinetic energy and speed far from the atomic nucleus, b≥0 is the impact parameter, and L is the magnitude of angular momentum. The nonrelativistic limit requires v≪c, with c the speed of light. The fixed-target approximation requires the target mass to be much greater than m. In SI, κ has units Jm, E has units J, and b has units m.

Nuclear radius bound from a Coulomb turning point (rmin​=zZe2/(4πε0​Ecm​))

Words: 73
Rutherford scattering OurBigBook.com
For a head-on repulsive Rutherford scattering encounter, relative kinetic energy becomes Coulomb potential energy at closest approach. With projectile charge ze and target charge Ze, conservation of energy gives the displayed separation. If the Coulomb description remains valid down to that separation, it bounds the target's interaction radius from above, treating the projectile as pointlike. For a stationary target of mass M and incident projectile mass m, use centre-of-mass energy Ecm​=MElab​/(M+m); neglecting nuclear recoil amounts to M≫m.

Rutherford impact-parameter relation (b=2Eκ​cot2θ​)

Words: 133
Rutherford scattering OurBigBook.com
Let θ be the scattering angle between incoming and outgoing velocities, so forward scattering is θ=0 and exact reversal is θ=π. Define the length a=κ/(2E). Then
b=acot2θ​​,θ=2arctanba​.
(65)
For b>0, this gives 0<θ<π; b=0 is the head-on limiting case θ=π. Large deflections select small impact parameters, rather than requiring every incident alpha particle to reverse.
A short derivation uses conservation of angular momentum and conservation of energy. Choose the polar angle ϕ=0 at closest approach, and write u=1/r. The Binet equation for the repulsive Coulomb potential gives
dϕ2d2u​+u=−L2mκ​,u=L2mκ​(ϵcosϕ−1),ϵ2=1+mκ22EL2​.
(66)
The last equality follows by substituting this orbit into E=mr˙2/2+L2/(2mr2)+κ/r. The hyperbola reaches infinity at ϕ=±ϕ∞​, with cosϕ∞​=1/ϵ. Its scattering angle is θ=π−2ϕ∞​, hence
cot2θ​=ϵ2−1​=κ2E/m​L​=κ2Eb​.
(67)
This proves the relation without assuming that the deflection is small. The symbol ϵ here is a dimensionless orbital parameter, distinct from ε0​.

Rutherford differential cross-section (dΩdσ​=16E2κ2​csc42θ​)

Words: 208 Articles: 1
Rutherford scattering OurBigBook.com
For an incident beam uniform across its relevant impact parameters, an incident annulus has area dσ=2πb∣db∣. Rotational symmetry maps it to outgoing solid angle dΩ=2πsinθdθ. The central-potential classical differential cross-section and the Rutherford impact-parameter relation therefore give
​dθdb​​=2a​csc22θ​,dΩdσ​=sinθb​​dθdb​​=4a2​csc42θ​=16E2κ2​csc42θ​​.
(68)
This is a differential scattering cross-section, with units of area per steradian, conventionally m2sr−1, not a detector count and not an area per degree. It applies for 0<θ<π, with a finite limiting value at π. Doubling incident kinetic energy divides it by four at fixed angle; doubling either electric charge number multiplies it by four.
A useful independent check integrates over all azimuths between two positive angles. For 0<θ1​<θ2​≤π,
σ[θ1​,θ2​]​=∫θ1​θ2​​dΩdσ​2πsinθdθ=πa2(cot22θ1​​−cot22θ2​​).
(69)
This equals the incident annulus area π(b12​−b22​) directly. A detector covering only a small patch at one angle does not collect this full azimuthal band.

Target normalization in Rutherford scattering rates (S∝NZ2)

Words: 83
Rutherford differential cross-section OurBigBook.com
At fixed incident flux, projectile energy and detector geometry, the Rutherford differential cross-section gives count rate S∝NZ2, where N is the target nuclei per unit area. Equal N gives a Z2 rate ratio. Equal foil mass per area instead gives Z2/A, with A the atomic mass number, while equal physical thickness also requires the material mass density. An empirical log-log plot with slope s supplies a different, experimentally normalized relation S∝As. These normalizations must be specified before comparing different target elements.

Thin-foil scattering counts (μ=Ninc​ns​ηΔΩdΩdσ​)

Words: 407 Articles: 1
Rutherford scattering OurBigBook.com
Let Ninc​ be the number of projectiles actually incident on the foil during an exposure, ns​ its foil areal number density, and η the probability of detecting an accepted particle. For a sufficiently small detector patch of area A at distance R from the scattering point, with its normal at angle ψ to the line of sight,
ΔΩ≃R2Acosψ​,μ(θ)≃Ninc​ns​ηΔΩdΩdσ​(θ).
(70)
The product ns​(dσ/dΩ)ΔΩ is a dimensionless scattering probability in this approximation; μ is an expected value of counts, so it need not be an integer. The approximation requires a nearly constant differential scattering cross-section and efficiency across the patch and incident beam. For finite acceptance use μ=Ninc​ns​∫detector​η(Ω)(dσ/dΩ)dΩ, including the incident beam's spread if appreciable. A screen facing the foil has ψ=0.
For an original numerical model, stipulate monoenergetic alpha particles with z=2, E=5.00MeV, and a gold target with Z=79. Use the rounded model constant e2/(4πε0​)=1.440MeVfm, where 1MeV=106 electronvolts and 1fm=10−15m. Thus κ=227.52MeVfm and a=22.752fm. Choose Ninc​=1011, ns​=1021m−2, η=1, and ΔΩ=10−3sr. For example, A=1mm2 facing the foil at R≃31.6mm gives this small-patch solid angle.
At θ=90∘, b=a and dσ/dΩ=a2=517.654fm2sr−1=5.17654bsr−1, using 1 barn =100fm2=10−28m2. The expected signal is μ≃51.8 counts. At 60∘ it is four times larger, about 207 counts. Doubling foil areal number density or detector solid angle doubles these expected signals as long as the approximations continue to hold.
An observation also contains backgrounds. For a stable source and matched geometry, an estimator is Cnet​=Cfoil​−(Tfoil​/Tblank​)Cblank​, where T denotes exposure duration. If source activity changes, normalize by incident exposure as well. Background subtraction removes an estimated background; it does not make finite counting fluctuations disappear.

Foil areal number density (ns​=nt)

Words: 71
Thin-foil scattering counts OurBigBook.com
The number of target chemical atoms per incident area along the beam. For a uniform foil at normal incidence, number density n and thickness t give ns​=nt, in m−2. At oblique incidence the traversed path must replace t. The single-encounter count model requires the chance of two significant deflections to be negligible and energy loss through the foil to be small. A small probability in one detector patch alone does not establish either condition.

Rutherford model

Words: 276
Atomic physics OurBigBook.com Tags: Atomic nucleus
The Rutherford model places a concentrated central electric charge inside a much larger chemical atom. In 1911, Ernest Rutherford argued that rare large deflections were predominantly single close encounters, rather than accumulated small deviations in a diffuse-charge atom. He treated the central electric charge as positive for calculation while noting that the scattering deductions did not establish its sign. He explicitly deferred atomic stability.[ref]
The physical inference is a compact region generating a strong electric field, not a miniature hard wall. Most impact parameters miss that region, while a small subset give large deflections. The model supplies a way to infer interior structure from outgoing angles, a central use of scattering throughout atomic physics and nuclear physics. This inference does not by itself specify electron quantum states or explain spectral lines.
The repulsive model also sets a probing scale. At closest approach, conservation of energy with zero radial velocity gives
E=2mrmin2​L2​+rmin​κ​,rmin​=a+a2+b2​.
(71)
For the numerical model above, even a head-on projectile turns at rmin​=2a=45.504fm. This is a calculated closest-approach distance, not a measured atomic nucleus radius. A point-charge fit can constrain how compact the scattering centre must be, but cannot directly resolve structure at distances the projectiles never reach.
The Rutherford differential cross-section must not be extrapolated to zero angle: the unscreened point model has a forward divergence, while real neutral chemical atoms exhibit the screening effect, finite beam acceptance, and accumulated small deflections. At very short separation, finite nuclear size and the nuclear force can change the interaction. Nuclear recoil changes the relation between laboratory and centre-of-mass angles for lighter targets; appreciable energy loss or repeated large deflections invalidates the simple thin-foil scattering counts. These limits delimit the calculation rather than supplying evidence for a nuclear contact collision in the early experiment.
